tier_reason: timings.txt in msf_gif-testing lists first-party wall times for msf_gif, gif_h and jo_gif with no CPU model, date or input description; the public harness (test.cpp, built by build.sh with clang -march=native -Os) times only msf_gif, so the baseline side of the comparison has no public benchmark code. First-party, partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'uses SSE where available to encode at hundreds of megabytes a second, several times faster than comparable gif libraries'. msf_gif-testing timings.txt (nine lines, first-party): jo_gif2 ~1160 s, jo_gif ~425 s, gif_h dithered ~315 s, gif_h dithered 7bpp ~240 s, gif_h ~75 s, msf_gif ~14 s, msf_gif simd ~8 s, msf_gif threaded ~4 s, msf_gif simd threaded ~2 s. Single-threaded scalar msf_gif vs gif_h: 5.4x undithered, 22.5x vs gif_h dithered (msf_gif always dithers, so the dithered line is the closer match); vs jo_gif 30x; single-threaded SSE build vs gif_h 9.4x (all derived from page data). The threaded lines compare multi-threaded msf_gif against single-threaded baselines and do not correspond to the shipped single-threaded library. No numbers against giflib, gifski or ffmpeg were found (gifski comparison is a TODO in notes.txt).
corrections.license: Dual: MIT or Unlicense-style public-domain dedication (text at the bottom of msf_gif.h)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: msf_gif-testing build.sh / build.bat: clang -march=native -std=c++17 -Os (MSVC /Ox and /O2 configs commented out); timings.txt does not say which configuration produced it
corrections.workload: Encoding the author's sample animations (in/ directory of msf_gif-testing; test.cpp lists 13 clips such as bouncy 576x360x417 frames and tiles 384x240x625 frames, quality 16, alpha threshold 128). timings.txt itself does not state the input set, so it is not certain that these are the clips behind the totals.
corrections.caveats: timings.txt is a nine-line first-party note with no hardware, date, compiler or input description, and the gif_h/jo_gif timing code is not in the public msf_gif-testing repo (test.cpp times msf_gif only). The label gif_h is presumably Charlie Tangora's gif.h, but the file does not say. The 'threaded' rows describe a multithreaded variant that the shipped msf_gif.h v2.4 does not contain (notes.txt says multithreading was left out), so only the ~14 s scalar and ~8 s SSE rows describe the library as published. Output size and quality differ between encoders (msf_gif uses a fixed constant-quality palette with ordered dithering and inter-frame delta encoding; the README's smaller-file and quality claims come with no size or PSNR numbers against gif.h or jo_gif). A Handmade Network post (blocked here, search snippet only) cites about 500 MB/s average and 300 MB/s worst case on an unnamed laptop, with no baseline. A gifski comparison is a TODO in notes.txt. The public-domain alternative has no patent grant.

notes: Numbers match timings.txt, but the record omitted the gif_h dithered (~315 s) and jo_gif2 (~1160 s) lines; I added them and separated the single-threaded rows from the threaded ones. Last commit 2025-09-10 (stale), 239 stars, licence dual MIT / public domain, all confirmed.

tier_reason: docs/perf.md gives the mtpng command line (cargo run --release, --repeat=10) and machines, but the libpng side has no published harness ('@fixme how did I measure those libpng times?'), libpng/zlib versions and flags are unstated, and the 2015 MacBook CPU is named only as '5th-gen Core i7 3.1 GHz'. First-party, partial methodology: C.

corrections.language: Rust (C API via the capi cargo feature and c/mtpng.h; builds cdylib/staticlib callable from C/C++)
corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md 'Old performance data' (2018-era), dual-4K screenshot at default options. Single-threaded vs libpng: MacBook Pro 2015 Linux x86_64 libpng gcc 850 ms vs mtpng 555 ms (1.53x); macOS libpng clang 943 ms vs 563 ms (1.67x); Xeon E5520 Linux libpng gcc 1695 ms vs 1124 ms (1.51x); Raspberry Pi 3B+ aarch64 4692 ms vs 4311 ms (1.09x); Raspberry Pi 3B+ armhf 5368 ms vs 6068 ms (mtpng 0.88x, slower). Multi-threaded vs single-threaded libpng: MacBook Linux 2 threads 302 ms (2.81x), 4 threads with HT 248 ms (3.43x); Xeon E5520 8 threads 165 ms (10.3x), 16 threads 155 ms (10.9x); Pi 3B+ armhf 4 threads 1875 ms (2.86x), aarch64 4 threads 1416 ms (3.31x). All ratios derived from page data; the 1.0x/1.8x/2.2x factors printed on the page are mtpng thread scaling relative to mtpng on one thread, not ratios against libpng. README: single-threaded ~30-40% faster than libpng (Rust 1.29.0, 26 Sept 2018). The '2026 data' section has mtpng times only (e.g. Apple M3 Max 237 ms on 1 thread, 23 ms on 16; Ryzen 9 5950X Linux 301 ms on 1 thread, 25 ms on 32) and no libpng column.
corrections.caveats: perf.md says '@fixme how did I measure those libpng times? need to recreate that', so the libpng baseline has no published harness, version, zlib build or flags, and all libpng numbers date from 2018. The work differs from libpng: mtpng's adaptive filter scores only Sub/Up/Average/Paeth (src/filter.rs filter_adaptive), while libpng 1.6's default PNG_ALL_FILTERS selection also scores None (pngwutil.c png_write_find_filter); the README says a 0.3.5 change (crates.io 2021-04-22, after these timings) altered the heuristic to match libpng in some cases, so the timed builds chose filters differently from libpng on the screenshot input. Deflate runs in independent 256 KiB chunks, which the README says compresses a tiny fraction worse than libpng. Multi-threaded rows are many threads against single-threaded libpng. On 32-bit ARM mtpng is slower than libpng single-threaded. The repository now lives at github.com/bvibber/mtpng (brion/mtpng redirects); crates.io's latest published version is 0.4.1 while the repo is at 0.5.0.

notes: Numbers and derived ratios check out against docs/perf.md; I split single-thread from multi-thread and added the Xeon and Raspberry Pi rows, including the armhf case where mtpng is slower. language is not in verify.py's CORRECTABLE set, and the repo moved to bvibber/mtpng, so the language and repo_url changes need a decisions.json override. Last commit 2026-06-08 (active), 228 stars, MIT, all confirmed.

tier_reason: The README table times the refreshed binary against ARM's official 64-bit astcenc and the Mali TCT 32-bit binary on one image on an Intel Core i5 760, with no benchmark script, block size, thread count, compiler or flags. First-party, partial methodology: C.

corrections.license: ARM End User Licence Agreement for the Mali ASTC Specification and Software Codec, version 1.3 (license.txt): non-OSI, use limited to the 'Authorised Purpose' of ASTC compression tools, no right to develop hardware; not Apache-2.0
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'about 2x faster than the Mali TCT binary and about 1.5x faster than the one from official repo'. Table for turret_diffuse_map.png on Intel Core i5 760 (seconds, Mali TCT 32-bit / official astcenc 64-bit / refreshed 64-bit): veryfast 0.41/0.39/0.19; fast 1.04/0.86/0.40; medium 6.11/4.36/3.20; thorough 22.90/14.98/11.54; exhaustive 52.56/30.99/25.23. Against the official 64-bit astcenc: 2.05x veryfast, 2.15x fast, 1.36x medium, 1.30x thorough, 1.23x exhaustive; against Mali TCT 1.91x-2.60x (derived from page data). The README's '1.5x' is about right only as an average: the slower, higher-quality presets gain 1.23x-1.36x.
corrections.caveats: Historical 2016 fork of the ARM 1.x evaluation codec; current ARM astc-encoder releases are a rewrite with SIMD and are far faster, so this is mainly an example of optimizing the old reference encoder. Quality is not matched or measured: the README claims 'some quality improvement' but gives no PSNR, and commit 00f9f3d ('Fix for finding best partitionings for 2planes mode') changes which partitions the dual-plane search excludes, so output differs from the baseline. The speedup otherwise comes from per-thread reuse of scratch buffers instead of per-block new/delete (b5a2d16) and batched block processing in encode_astc_image_threadfunc (4766689). One image, one CPU; block size, thread count, compiler and flags are not stated; the Mali TCT comparison is a 32-bit binary against a 64-bit one. Licence is ARM's custom EULA, so reference only. An identical README is in the abusenius/refreshed-astc-encoder fork.

notes: Table numbers and derived ratios verified against the README. The licence is ARM's Mali ASTC codec EULA v1.3, not Apache-2.0, so usability stays reference. The speed claim is not at matched quality: a search bug fix changes output and no PSNR is reported. Last commit 2016-06-12 (abandoned), 1 star, fork of ARM-software/astc-encoder, all confirmed.
